In granting preliminary plan approval, the Commission waived a number of requirements and required that the applicant return for final plan review with a complete submission – for action (AP 26 Lot 234 zoned M-MU 75; AP 27 Lots 36 and 269 zoned M-1, Valley) Mr. Manjrekar introduced the request for final plan approval where the applicant had returned to the CPC at their request, to present a complete submission of the plan where items were waived at the preliminary plan stage. Attorney Nicholas Goodier and engineers Dana Nisbet and Paul Bannon presented the plan on the applicant’s behalf. Ms. Nisbet presented the final plan and spoke about the general site plan in addition to the drainage plan, submission of state approvals, the lighting plan and landscaping. Mr. Gazdacko asked if the second phase with the apartment building would be progressing. Mr. Goodier said it would occur pending a zone change to allow for residential use by right. Mr. Bannon presented the traffic study and spoke about traffic infrastructure changes, safety enhancements and interior site circulation. A discussion on traffic and environmental protection ensued. Mr. Manjrekar read out the DPDs staff report which found that the applicant had submitted the items that the CPC waived at the preliminary plan stage and that the submission conformed to the zoning ordinance and comprehensive plan. ACTION Upon a motion by Commissioner Verdi, seconded by Commissioner Potter, the CPC voted to approve the final plan based on their findings. In accordance with their actions, the plan was approved subject to the following conditions: 1. The CPC approved the final plan for phase one, finding that it conformed to the zoning ordinance and comprehensive plan. 2. The applicant shall apply for an administrative subdivision to configure the lot as depicted on the plan. 3. The landscaping plan shall be subject to the approval of the Forester. 4. Processing of the final plan approval was delegated to DPD staff. 4 The CPC voted as follows: Aye: N. Verdi, C. Potter, H. Bilodeau, M. Cordero, M. Gazdacko DEVELOPMENT PLAN REVIEW 4. Meeting Minutes of March 9, 2020: Mr. Marsella made a motion, seconded by Ms. Hampton, to approve the meeting minutes. Members Gelnett, Schoettle, Marsella, Rivera, Hampton, and Chille voted in favor. Acceptance of DDRC 2021 Meeting Schedule: Mr. Marsella made a motion, seconded by Ms. Rivera, to accept the DDRC 2021 meeting schedule. Members Gelnett, Schoettle, Marsella, Rivera, Hampton, and Chille voted in favor. PROJECT REVIEW 1. DRC Application No. 19.36: 151-155 Chestnut Street – Conceptual and Final Design Review (combined stages) Proposal by Providence Chestnut 1, LLC, to demolish the existing structures located at 151 Chestnut Street and 155 Chestnut Street, and to construct a new 10-story, mixed-use building at 151-155 Chestnut Street. The Committee previously granted conceptual and final approval for a new 12-story, mixed used building, including demolition waivers, a development incentive in the form of a 30% height bonus, and waivers from Zoning Ordinance Sections 606.A.4 (Building Height and Massing/Recess Line) and 606.E.1 (Building Facades/Ground Floor Transparency). On appeal from conceptual approval, the Superior Court reversed the DDRC’s decision to grant the 30% height bonus, but upheld all other approvals. The matter is before the DDRC on remand for design review and approval of a 9-story structure. The proposed design is identical to the previously-approved project, but does not require a height bonus. Attorney Rob Stolzman gave a brief overview and introduced Todd Benson, applicant, and Randy Gerner, architect. Mr. Stolzman explained that the demolition and design waivers were upheld by court order with the exception of the height bonus, which the applicant has removed the height bonus. He then made a comparison between the prior approved plans and the revised plans absent the height bonus. Mr. Gerner made a powerpoint presentation. He presented the plans for the 9-story building, noting that the design is the same as the previously taller building. In response to a question by Mr. Stolzman, Mr. Gerner replied that there have been no changes to the site plan as previously approved. He then showed the comparison between the 9-story building and the 12-story building, noting that the design is the same except for the top 3 stories. Mr. Gerner presented building elevations comparing the present design with the design presented at the March 9 th DDRC meeting, noting the same materials and the amount of shadow changes. Mr. Stolzman remarked that it is administratively the same as approved with the exception of the height bonus, adding that it is in conformance with prior approvals. At this time, public comment was taken. Olin Thompson commented that the applicant had initially stated that a 99’ tall building was not financially practical. NEW BUSINESS Item 8 – Motion to approve the borrowing of an amount up to $2,000,000.00 to complete purchase of 35 Hemlock Street. Sam Budway provided a brief history of the property, which has been owned by The Narragansett Bay Commission for several years and was purchased by PRA to accommodate longtime tenant Al-Jacs and provide additional space for Capco Steel. The purchase assists in job retention and the creation of new jobs with the company expansion. A portion of the lot will also be used as ancillary parking for the Paul Cuffee School. Attorney Sandra Mack provided details around the borrowing and leasing of the property, which includes the borrowing of up to $2M with variable interest [approximately 4%]. The 10 year lease includes an administrative fee that will pay the debt service and provide a reserve. The closing is set for the 24th and is to be recorded on the 27th. Councilman Taylor made a motion to approve as presented and Patricia Moran seconded the motion. The motion was passed unanimously. As the master landlord at the Port, all lease extensions must be approved by the PRA. Lehigh Cement has requested a 30 year lease extension to 2054. The current lease ends in 2024. The extension is requested, as public and private financing with infrastructure improvements required the extended term. This tenant is high producing and continues to grow. Councilman Taylor made a motion to approve as presented and Patricia Moran seconded the motion. The motion was passed unanimously. Sam Budway reported on the 3 bids that were received from the construction RFP: Low bidder – Tower Construction approximately $4.6M Tavares Construction approximately $5.1M Marin Construction approximately $5.8M The low bidder failed to submit/provide 5 of the required forms, including financial statements and cost breakdowns, and was therefore disqualified for non -compliance. Tavares Construction was the lowest responsible bidder. Final approval of the bidder will go to Rhode Island Housing construction oversight team, who has given a verbal approval for the award. The owners representative for the project is Brian Byrnes, Deputy Superintendent of Parks with assistance from the architect, InForm Studios. Bonnie Nickerson added that the project is fully funded. BILLS AND COMMUNICATIONS Mr. Budway reported on: Item 8 – Mack Law Associates – legal matters December 2019 Item 9- Darrow Everett, LLP – legal matters November 2019 Item 10 – Libby Slater Interior Design – design services 50 Sims Ave TO BE RATIFIED Item 11 – Mack Law Associates – legal matters November 2019 Patricia Moran made a motion to approve the bill as presented and Manuel Cordero seconded the motion. The motion was passed unanimously. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR’S REPORT Item 12 – Mr. Budway, in Bonnie Nickerson’s absence, stated there is no report at this time. No action was taken by the Board. NEW BUSINESS Item 13 – Motion to authorize a reimbursement agreement for remediation work related to 345 Harris Avenue. The property at 345 Harris Avenue, the former 6th district court house, was previously owned by PRA. The buyer had engaged with a firm to demolish the structure and the scope of work was not complete [failed to abate asbestos and mold and properly remove debris from the foundation]. DEM fined the property owner. PRA is jointly responsible for the fines, as we were still the owners of the property at the time of demolition [not advised of the demolition taking place during the purchase & sale due diligence period]. Payment of $112,500 represents 50% of the environmental remediation cost, sharing liability with the now owner. Discussion continued regarding concerns that this could happen again and plans to ensure protection of the agency if this type of action takes place. Sam stated he will be working with legal council to limit access to future buyers properties prior to closing. Manuel Cordero made a motion approve as presented and Jesse Kenner seconded the motion. The motion was passed unanimously. Item 14 – Motion to authorize Executive Director to negotiate a lease and/or purchase and sales agreement for 22 Rye Street The property is a former school that is vacant and owned by the city. The city is to transfer to the PRA for redevelopment. We are seeking authorization to acquire property and the ability to enter into a lease or P&S with a future developer. Currently we are working to figure out the best re-use of the property. Discussion involved comments from board members Rodriguez and Cordero regarding costs of maintaining the building, ideal use and the possibility of using this property as swing space to deal with the PSD issues. Patricia Moran made a motion to approve as presented and Jesse Kenner seconded the motion. The motion was passed unanimously. Item 15- Motion to authorize executive director to negotiate and execute a lease for 50 Sims Avenue. PRA has applied for and received a $1M forgivable loan and is applying for a $3.5M EDA grant for the 50 Sims Avenue tenant fit out. The Beauty Shoppe, a Pittsburgh developer, is the planned master developer/partner. TBS primary business includes co-working space and build outs/real estate development making them a prime candidate to be a lease and development partner. We are proposing to develop a long term lease at 50 Sims Avenue for TBS to develop on our behalf. PRA would retain ownership and the entity would sub-lease. Discussion ensued regarding the break-even point and assurance of a viable project model. Diego Rodriguez made a motion to approve as presented and Jesse Kenner seconded the motion. The motion was passed unanimously. Item 16 – Motion to authorize executive director to negotiate and execute a loan agreement, promissory note and mortgage for construction at 267 Veazie Street. The city of Providence, through the Community Development division has been involved with CDBG dollars to renovate the property. Smith Hill CDC is overseeing the redevelopment. They are seeking a $23k loan for a ten year period [to be part of the permanent debt] on the project. When the house was initially painted in the renovation the paint was not sustainable and did not meet federal regulations, therefor, the house required repainting and siding [at a cost of $23k]. It was noted the initial painting was “faulty” and “misapplied”. Patricia Moran made a motion to approve as presented and Manuel Cordero seconded the motion. The motion was passed unanimously. Mr. Budway indicated the conclusion of the meeting. Jesse Kenner made a motion to adjourn the meeting. Diego Rodriguez seconded the motion. The motion passed unanimously. The meeting adjourned at 4:39 PM.

Referral 3494 – Rezoning of 45-47 America Street Petitioner: DNC Acquisitions LLC The petitioner is requesting to rezone 45-47 America Street from R-3 to R-4 with certain conditions – for action (AP 28 Lot 236, Federal Hill) Mr. Azar introduced the item, a request to rezone the lot R-4 with no zoning restrictions to allow for 14 dwelling units. The request was similar to ones seen around the City where the R-4 zoning was used to increase density in certain areas. Mr. Nicholas Goodier represented the applicant and said the number of units would increase but the number of bedrooms would not. He said the comprehensive plan supported the increased density. A discussion on the building and configuration of the units ensued. Mr. Azar said the site is composed of two buildings that will be connected. He shared the plans to explain the proposed changes. Mr. Quezada asked if the applicant intended to implement similar changes for other properties they owned. Mr. Goodier said there were no current plans. Ms. West said the demand for new units was driven by smaller household size and the change would support that trend. Mr. Azar read out the staff report and recommended that the CPC make a positive recommendation to the City Council, finding the change to be in conformance with the zoning ordinance and comprehensive plan. On a motion by Commissioner Gazdacko, seconded by Commissioner Bilodeau, the CPC voted to recommend that the City Council approve the proposed zone change to R-4 with the conditions that the dimensional standards of table 4-1 do not apply to the lot. In accordance with their action, the CPC recommends that the zone change be approved subject to the following condition: The applicant shall make an effort to introduce pervious surface on the site and meet the canopy coverage requirement by making plantings under the supervision of the City Forester. 3 The CPC voted as follows: Aye: M. Referral No. 3501 – Prohibition of bulk storage of liquid propane gas Proponent: Councilman Pedro Espinal The proponent is proposing to amend Article 12 of the ordinance to prohibit bulk storage of liquid propane gas in all zones – for action Mr. Azar introduced the item, which would prohibit the bulk storage of liquid propane throughout the City. He said the amendment appeared to be motivated by a plan to expand a storage facility in the Port of Providence. Ms. West said it would have been beneficial to hear from the Councilman. Mr. Azar said there is a concern about industrial uses in the port and their impacts on the Community in addition to concerns about expansion of fossil fuel infrastructure and safety. Mr. Gazdacko asked if the amendment would make the existing propane facility nonconforming. Mr. Azar said it would be the case and prevent expansion. A discussion on the implications of the recommendation and its relationship to the comprehensive plan ensued. Mr. Quezada asked if currently vested applications would be affected by the change. Mr. Azar said they would be unaffected. Mr. Quezada asked if there was a mechanism to add more requirements to a special use permit requirement. Mr. Azar said the CPC could do so and the CPC added some items to their recommendation. A discussion on recommendations ensued. Mr. Steve Ahlquist said the change would increase the number of trucks and amount of propane brought in by trains and that there were health concerns for residents. Recommendation On a motion by Commissioner Bilodeau, seconded by Commissioner Verdi, the CPC voted to recommend that the City Council should not prohibit the subject use, but have it be subject to Special Use Permit. In addition to the special use permit criteria, other criteria that could be imposed include those related to fire safety or leak protection, air pollution, transportation pollution and the ability to adapt the infrastructure to other fuels. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: H. Bilodeau, N. Verdi, M. Quezada, M. Cordero, M. Gazdacko, C. West MAJOR LAND DEVELOPMENT PROJECT PUBLIC INFORMATIONAL MEETING 3. The meeting was called to order by Chairman Paul DePetrillo. The Secretary called the roll and noted the following members were present: Present: Paul DePetrillo - Chairman Robert DeGregorio – Vice-Chairman Salvatore Deluise Lorraine Byrne Walter Augustyn Constance Beck – Alternate Absent: Julie Finn – Alternate Also present: David Petrarca, Esq., City Solicitor Daniel Geagan, Warwick Planning Department Mary Ellen Hall - Stenographer Amy Cota, Secretary The Chairman asked if there were any petitions to be WITHDRAWN or CONTINUED. There being none, the Chairman called the first petition. Petition #10752 Ward 3 1850 Post Rd. The petition of Landing Partners, LLC, 600 Madison Ave., 24th Floor, New York, NY, and SHIVA, LLC, 655 Washington Street, Weymouth, MA, request a dimensional variance to convert the existing hotel into 203 dwelling units, having less than required parking spaces, and less than required driveway/travel width. Assessor’s Plat 322, Lot 339, zoned Gateway (G). K. Joseph Shekarchi, Esq. was present and representing the petitioners. Regular hearing of November 9, 2021 Page 2 Daniel Geagan from the Planning Department read the recommendations into the record. Attorney Shekarchi stated he reviewed the stipulations, and his client agrees to all stipulations presented. Attorney Shekarchi stated the petitioners are here tonight for parking relief only. There is a critical need for housing in the City, and the proposal is to convert the existing hotel into 203 dwelling units. There were concerns raised about the ratio of parking not being sufficient to support the 203 dwelling units, but after working with the Planning Department, the petitioner’s agreed to reduce the number of units from 203 to 181 units, which is comparable to other apartment complexes in the city. The Chairman asked if there was anyone present in opposition or in favor of the petition. There being none, Robert DeGregorio stated the hardship is unique due to the use formerly being a hotel, it won’t alter the general characteristics of the surrounding area, and the conversion will help economics in the area. The motion was seconded by Lorraine Byrne, and passed unanimously by the Board that the petition be GRANTED WITH STIPULATIONS. Petition #10746 Ward 8 800 Toll Gate Rd. The petition of Warwick Family Dental Group, LLC & MSS Twelve Realty, LLC, 800 Toll Gate Rd., Warwick, RI, requests an amendment to a previously approved petition to convert the attached garage into additional patient rooms, and a lab for the existing dentist office. Assessor’s Plat 260, Lot 43, zoned Residential A-40. K. Joseph Shekarchi, Esq. was present and representing the petitioners. Attorney Shekarchi stated the property was previously granted approval from this Board to utilize the property as a dental office. The petitioners are looking to expand the dental practice by converting the attached garage into additional patient rooms and a dental lab. Lorraine Byrne asked if the property was connected to sewers. Munal Salem, Petitioner, was present and sworn in by the Chairman. Mr. Salem stated they are in favor of connecting to city sewers, but it is their understanding sewers are not available in that area of Toll Gate Road. The petitioners agreed to the stipulation that if sewers become available, they will connect. Regular hearing of November 9, 2021 Page 3 Ms. Byrne stated according to the plans, it looks like they are adding two chairs in that back patio area. She asked if the patio area is currently utilized. Mr. Salem stated it is currently occupied as a private office for the doctor. Ms. Byrne stated she went by the subject property earlier in the day, and the parking lot was full. She asked if all of these areas were included in the parking calculations. Mark Chase, West Brookfield, MA, was present and sworn in by the Chairman. Attorney Shekarchi stated Mark Chase prepared and put together the application. Mr. Chace stated he did include all of the areas in the parking calculations. The Chairman asked if there was anyone present in opposition or in favor of the petition. There being none, Robert DeGregorio stated the petitioners agreed to the stipulation to connect to sewers should they become available, and made a motion to approve the petition, seconded by Lorraine Byrne, and passed unanimously by the Board that the petition be GRANTED WITH STIPULATIONS. West Recuse: H Bilodeau ACTION – Master Plan Upon a motion by Commissioner Gazdacko seconded by Commissioner Verdi, the CPC voted to approve the master plan subject to the following conditions: 1. Case No. 21-035MA – 659 – 663 Admiral Street and 22 Glocester Street Applicant: Strive Realty Owner: Citadel Properties LLC The applicant is requesting master plan approval to construct a five story mixed-use building with commercial on the ground floor and 45 residences on the upper stories in the C-1 zone. The applicant is requesting a dimensional adjustment for parking where 45 spaces are required and 27 will be provided. A dimensional adjustment for height is also requested where a height of 60’ and five stories is proposed – for action (AP 123 Lots 165 and 166 zoned C-1, AP 123 Lot 171 zoned R-2, Wanskuck) – A transcript of the item is available by request and has been made part of the record Mr. Manjrekar introduced the item. Mr. Dylan Conley, an attorney, presented on behalf of the applicant. A discussion on the item ensued with the CPC hearing from the applicant, their experts and the public. Mr. Potter made a motion, seconded by Mr. Bilodeau to continue the item to the December 12 CPC meeting. All voted in favor. MINOR LAND DEVELOPMENT PROJECT 3. Case No. 21-037MI – 113 Ives Street Applicant: 113 Ives LLC The applicant is proposing to demolish an existing building and construct a four story multifamily dwelling with 16 units in the C-1 zone – for action (AP 17 Lot 460, Fox Point) Mr. Azar introduced the item, a proposal to build a four story, 16 unit development on a lot that measured 3 approximately 2,500 SF in the C-1 zone, which does not restrict the number of dwelling units per lot and has no offstreet parking requirements. The project was in compliance with the zoning ordinance. Architect Kevin Diamond and Owner Dustin Dezube presented the project on behalf of the applicant. They presented development plans and spoke about the site’s layout and the building’s design, which was intended to conform to the neighborhood aesthetic. The changes would apply to development plan review (DPR), administrative officers, and the Downtown Design Review Committee (DDRC) which would be a body that conducts DPR. Regulations for administrative subdivisions would remain the same. Minor subdivisions would apply to creation of up to nine lots and would be reviewed administratively. The CPC would review minor subdivisions that require relief. The enabling act allows communities to set thresholds beyond what is provided in state law. Minor land development projects currently include only residential development, but the changes would allow for some mixed use with commercial to be considered minor. He said projects that required dimensional adjustments and variances would appear before the CPC. He asked if design waivers could be granted by DPD staff. Mr. Gazdacko said design waivers could be classified as major and minor. A discussion on changes ensued. Mr. Azar said there would be two categories of waivers, minor and major, where major requests would appear before the board. He said the distinction between major and minor changes would also be included in the draft of the regulations. Mr. Azar said the DDRC conducts DPR and would be considered a technical review committee. Unified Development Review is mandated for all communities and would continue without changes under the new regulations. The CPC was considering if a mechanism for public notice would be provided for by-right projects. Ms. Verdi said projects could be uploaded to the website. Mr. Azar said the master plan stage for land development projects would be a public hearing and the preliminary plan would only require notice to direct abutters. Citizens could subscribe to the secretary of state’s website for updates on CPC meetings. Mr. Azar said design waivers and dimensional adjustments are to be granted at the discretion of the CPC and the regulations would clarify how the CPC can mitigate negative impacts from adjustments. He spoke about how regulations for major and minor changes could be crafted in the context of projects. Mr. Sanchez asked how projects under 10,000 SF would be reviewed. Mr. Azar said it would be reviewed as staff level DPR. Mr. Doug Victor said neighborhood committee chairs should be included in the process to update regulations. Mr. Gazdacko said the changes were mandated by state law and neighborhood groups could participate in the comprehensive plan update process. DEVELOPMENT PLAN REVIEW 3. DEVELOPMENT PLAN REVIEW COMMITTEE ▪ “5 Aborn Street” PUBLIC MEETING Preliminary Plan Proposal: Adaptive Reuse of an existing building using first floor for two (2) commercial garage units and the upper floors for two (2) residential units. Requires waivers for landscaping, drainage, sidewalks, and curbs. Zoning: C-3 (General Business) AP 1, Lot 30 5 Aborn Street Attorney Robert Murray and applicant Anthony Albanese Jr., principal of Bridgebrook LLC, presented a proposal for the adaptive reuse of the property located at 5 Aborn Street within the Pawtuxet Village area. The applicant explained that the property has historically presented redevelopment challenges due to its location within a flood zone and the constraints associated with the existing C-3 zoning district. The proposal consists of retaining the existing structure and redeveloping the site with two enclosed commercial parking spaces on the ground level and two residential units above. The applicant stated that the residential -over- commercial configuration is a permitted use under the zoning ordinance and was pursued through the City’s adaptive reuse provisions. Page 2 of 3 (401) 780-3136 | https://www.cranstonri.gov/departments/planning/ Mr. Murray provided background on the property and the Albanese family’s long -term investment in maintaining and improving properties throughout Pawtuxet Village. He noted that prior redevelopment efforts at the site had encountered challenges over the yea rs and stated that the current proposal was designed to work within the limitations of the site and applicable floodplain regulations. Committee Discussion: Stanley Pikul asked whether the adaptive reuse provisions limited the project to uses already permitted within the zoning district and noted that a traditional two -family residential structure would not trigger the same sprinkler requirements as a mixed -use building. T he applicant confirmed that the proposed use complies with the existing zoning regulations and acknowledged the additional building code requirements associated with a mixed-use structure. Mr. Pikul also requested confirmation regarding the existence of an elevation certificate for the property. The applicant stated that an elevation certificate had been prepared by Waterman Engineering and would be submitted during the permitting process. Additional discussion occurred regarding the proposed flood vents and flood mitigation measures, with the applicant confirming that engineered flood vent systems had been incorporated into the design in accordance with code requirements. SMILEY City Plan Commission Minutes of the July 15, 2025 meeting A meeting of the City Plan Commission (CPC) was held on Tuesday, July 15, 2025 at 4:45 pm in the Joseph Doorley Municipal Building, 444 Westminster Street, 1st floor Meeting Room, Providence RI 02903 A video recording of the meeting is available at: https://www.youtube.com/@pvdepc Opening Session Call to order: Chair Michael Gazdacko called the meeting to order at 4:47 pm Members Present: Michael Gazdacko, David Caldwell, Noel Sanchez, Charlotte Lipschitz, Miguel Quezada, Rachael Dotson Members Absent: Cyd McKenna Staff Present: Robert Azar, Deputy Director, Choyon Manjrekar, Principal Planner, Megan DiSanto, Deputy City Solicitor Approval of minutes from the June 17, 2025 meeting: On a motion by Commissioner Quezada seconded by Commissioner Sanchez, the CPC voted to approve the minutes. All voted in favor. Directors Report: Mr. Azar said a design committee had been convened and met to discuss design standards for residential development and would consider regulations for mixed use and commercial development in the future. The General Assembly passed a number of bills related to land use and development that would be studied and incorporated in the Zoning Ordinance and Development Review Regulations. CITY COUNCIL REFERRAL 1. Referral no 3601 – 1 Charles Street Petitioner: 1 Charles LLC The petitioner is requesting a rezoning of the subject lot from R-4 to D-I-45 – for vote (AP 3 Lot 616, Charles) Mr. Manjrekar introduced the item and said the petitioner was requesting to rezone the lot from R-4 to D-I-45 so that a short term rental use within the building could continue without being owned occupied as required in the R-4 zone. Petitioner Carlos Varum appeared before the CPC with attorney Jeff Padwa. Mr. Padwa said the property was being used for short term rentals since 2022 and is adjacent to mostly commercial areas. Mr. Manjrekar read out the DPD's staff report which recommended that the CPC make a positive recommendation to the City Council. NEW BUSINESS Item 16- Vote to re-designate 220 Blackstone Street by change of covenants and allow transfer of the properties and change in use from medical offices to housing. The former Flynn School at 220 Blackstone was designated to The Aspen Group for redevelopment in 2016 through public process. In 2023 the site remained vacant and in the inerim years they discovered that medical use and market rate housing were not viable at the site. Aspen recently came to the PRA with a new developer that can purchase the property and develop it. For this to go forward, the Agency will need to allow the transfer from Aspen to Marathon Development and change the use to mixed income housing. The 2018 purchase and sale provides for a condition to allow PRA to buy back if development is not completed in a certain timeframe. Rather than a buy back, the PRA would allow the change of hands and use change for a fee of $250k to the Agency. The allowance of this transfer would speed up the development timeline, which has been lying dormant for many years. If approved, the transfer would include the continued the same covenants and reverter clause as the previous arrangement. It will then be vetted by The Aspen Group and Marathon Developments attorneys. The agreement will be contingent on financing, with an option to purchase by June 30, 2024. Item 8 - Vote to approve Department of Housing & Human Services request to utilize local housing Trust balance in amount of $380,859.38 for very low-income housing. Housing and Human Services Director, Emily Freedman outlined the request for funds to be used to negate a portion of 2011 Neighborhood Stabilization funding for 80-120% AMI housing. When the federal government closed the program, it was noted that the federal requirement was not met, and funding was to be used for 50% AMI to meet the overall goals. To close out the grant, and not have to pay the money back, the city needs to now complete a 50% AMI project and cannot use other federal funds in the project. The goal of the federal program aligns with PRA goals. A contribution from the Providence Housing Trust of $380,859.38 would pair with the remaining NSP balance to fund a project to meet the requirements and fulfill all obligations. If approved, an RFP will be issued with the new affordable housing requirements to enable us to fund a new rehabilitation project within the city to provide affordable housing. Noting that current projects are ineligible. The timing would be an RFP late this month with spring construction. This is a housing trust investment and PRA will review the RFP. City Plan Commission Minutes of the August 30, 2022 meeting A meeting of the City Plan Commission (CPC) was held on Tuesday, August 30, 2022 at 4:45 pm in the Joseph Doorley Municipal Building, 444 Westminster Street, Law Department Conference Room, Second Floor, Suite 220, Providence RI 02903 A video recording of the meeting is available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YpjzzzzTHSY and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jG9UtH-VBNo Opening Session Call to order: Chair Michael Gazdacko called the meeting to order at 4:49 pm Members Present: Michael Gazdacko, Chair, Harrison Bilodeau, Noel Sanchez, Christian Potter, Manuel Cordero, Nicole Verdi Members Absent: Miguel Quezada Staff Present: Robert Azar, Deputy Director, Choyon Manjrekar, Principal Planner, Lisa Dinerman, Senior Assistant City Solicitor Approval of minutes from the June 28, July 19 and August 16 meetings: Mr. Bilodeau made a motion seconded by Commissioner Verdi to approve the minutes. All voted in favor. Director’s report: Mr. Azar said the October meeting would be held on October 11 due to the meeting room being used for early voting. MINOR SUBDIVISION 1. Case no. 22-039MI – 175-177 Webster Ave Applicant: Kenol Cadet The applicant is proposing to subdivide the 10,000 SF lot, which is zoned R-3, into two lots of 5,000 SF – for action (AP 108 Lot 527, Silver Lake) Mr. Manjrekar introduced the item. Mr. Nabil Rashid, the surveyor, represented the applicant. He said the plan conformed to the zoning ordinance and was drawn to conform to dimensional and setback requirements. Mr. Manjrekar read out the DPD’s staff report and recommended that the CPC approved the plan finding it to be in conformance with the zoning ordinance and comprehensive plan. Upon a motion by Commissioner Bilodeau seconded by Commissioner Verdi, the CPC voted to approve the preliminary plan finding it to be in conformance with the zoning ordinance and comprehensive plan. The plan was approved subject to the following conditions: 1. The validity of the preliminary plan is extended to one year from the date of recording of the approval 2 letter. 2. Final plan approval was delegated to DPD staff. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: H. Bilodeau, N. Verdi, C. Potter, M. Cordero, M. Gazdacko Abstain: N. Sanchez Mayor Jorge Elorza joined the meeting and commended the Commission for their service. DEVELOPMENT PLAN REVIEW 2. Case No. 2022-10 DPR – 135 Prairie Ave Applicant: Community Preparatory School The applicant is proposing to amend the campus master plan for construction of a new building providing approximately 11,159 SF which will contain a gymnasium with a support stage, office and restrooms. The applicant is seeking dimensional waivers for locating multiple buildings on a lot, multiple curb cuts and curb cut width. Changes to site landscaping and parking are also proposed. The site is zoned R-3 – for action (AP 23 lots 227,997,992,991 and 596, Upper South Providence) Mr. Manjrekar introduced the item and the associated design waivers. Ms. Kathy Bartels, the architect, Dan Corley, Head of School and Mark Hollis, and engineer, presented the plan on the applicant’s behalf. Ms. Bartels presented the plans to construct an arts and athletic center on four campus lots that would be merged. The building would have a footprint of approximately 11,000 SF with a capacity of about 700 people. No new parking requirements would be triggered. She said that design waivers were required for driveway width and situating multiple buildings on a lot. Mr. Cordero asked how students would move through campus. Ms. Bartels said there would be an internal walkway to allow for movement. Mr. Azar said the development conformed to the dimensional requirements of the ordinance. Mr. Sanchez asked how the building would affect nearby traffic with placement of the curb cut. Ms. Bartels said there would be landscaping and building features that interacted with the street. Mr. Manjrekar read out the DPD’s staff report which found the building to conform to the ordinance’s requirements. He recommended that the CPC grant the requested design waivers. Ms. Carla Destefano said she was a neighbor in support of the project. Mr. Potter said he was in support of the project and had family members who attended the school. A discussion on the project ensued. Upon a motion by Commissioner Verdi seconded by Commissioner Potter the CPC voted to approve the design waivers from the restriction of the number of principal structures on a lot, and curb cut width. The CPC approved the development plan, finding that the applicant satisfactorily demonstrated compliance with the requirements outlined in Section 1202.M of the zoning ordinance pertaining to Development Plan Review for Primary or Secondary Educational Facilities. In accordance with their action, the plan was approved subject to the following condition: The applicant shall merge the subject lots. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: N. Verdi, C. Potter, H. Bi

Mr. Brennan stated they have been working with the Planning Department, and are in agreement with the stipulations being placed on the approval. Mr. Dylan Conley, an attorney, and Mr. Kevin Diamond, an architect, presented on behalf of the petitioner. Mr. Conley explained that the proposed development will contain three market-rate units and six workforce units. When the petitioner applied, Mr. Conley explained, the City’s C-1 zone was more advantageous for increasing residential density than its R-4 zone, compelling the applicant to apply for a C-1 rezoning with a zoning footnote to limit future development on the site to residential uses exclusively. Mr. Diamond noted that the design team conceived the project with C-1 standards in mind. Mr. Conley expressed discomfort over rezoning the parcels into R-4 instead of C-1, as it could compromise his 5 petitioner’s original design. Mr. Conley also said that the petitioner was willing to condition the rezoning on the constructed housing being affordable at 120% AMI. Discussion ensued. Mr. Azar read out the staff report, noting that the City has moved away from rezoning areas to C-1 with a footnote to build higher density residential; an R-4 with laxer restriction has supplanted the old method. He also explained that the new R-4 zone’s rules better suit neighborhood applications such as 22-26 Ringgold as compared to the C-1 method. Discussion ensued. Commissioner Gazdacko opened the meeting to public comment. Commissioner Gazdacko registered his agreement with the staff report recommendation to recommend a rezone to R-4 instead of C-1. Discussion ensued about whether a suggestion of workforce housing could be included in the recommendation to the City Council. On a motion by Commissioner Bilodeau, seconded by Commissioner Potter, the CPC voted to recommend that the City Council rezone the subject lots to R-4, finding that it would be appropriate for this site, and in conformance with the zoning ordinance and comprehensive plan. The CPC also recommends that the Council adopt the proposed changes to the R-4 zone when amending the zoning ordinance. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: H. Bilodeau, C. Potter, N. Sanchez, M. City Plan Commission Minutes of the October 11, 2022 meeting A meeting of the City Plan Commission (CPC) was held on Tuesday, October 11, 2022 at 4:45 pm in the Joseph Doorley Municipal Building, 444 Westminster Street, 1st floor meeting room, Providence RI 02903 A video recording of the meeting is available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UGlCPA5DKCs Opening Session Call to order: Nicole Verdi acted as chair and called the meeting to order at 4:50 pm Members Present: Michael Gazdacko, Chair (arrived at 5:01 pm), Nicole Verdi, Harrison Bilodeau, Noel Sanchez, , Manuel Cordero, Miguel Quezada (arrived at 5:10 pm) Members Absent: Christian Potter Staff Present: Robert Azar, Deputy Director, Choyon Manjrekar, Principal Planner, Lisa Dinerman, Senior Assistant City Solicitor Approval of minutes from the September 20 meetings: Mr. Manjrekar said approval of the minutes would be deferred to the next meeting. Director’s report: Mr. Azar said a special meeting would be held on October 18. MINOR LAND DEVELOPMENT PROJECT – REQUEST FOR EXTENSION 1. Case No. 22-008MI – 153-165 Gano Street Applicant: Coastway Management LLC Mr. John Garrahy represented the applicant. Mr. Manjrekar said the CPC had granted an extension when it reviewed the item, but the applicant was before the board to formally request the extension in writing. On a motion by Commissioner Bilodeau, seconded by Commissioner Sanchez, the CPC voted to grant a one year extension of the validity of the project. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: H. Bilodeau, N. Sanchez , M. Cordero, N. Verdi 2 DEVELOPMENT PLAN REVIEW 2. Case No. 2022-11 DPR – 250 Lloyd Ave Applicant: Moses Brown School The applicant is proposing to amend the campus master plan for improvements to the athletic facilities which will include installation of a scoreboard with video capabilities and updates to the seating areas and playing fields. The amendment will not include installation of lighting – for action (AP 11 lots 48 and 132, College Hill) Mr. Manjrekar introduced the item. Ms. Amy Goins, an attorney, introduced the item on behalf of the applicant. Ron Dalgliesh, interim head of school, Peter Arpin, director of operations, Aj Kizekai, athletic director and consultant John Amato also presented for the applicant. Mr. Dalgliesh presented a slideshow outlining the proposed changes and spoke about the need for a scoreboard. He said the use of a video component was contingent on the zoning ordinance being changed to allow for it by right. Mr. Amato, a civil engineer, spoke about how the effects on neighboring property would be mitigated. Mr. Kizekai spoke about the proposed uses of the scoreboard. A discussion of activity on campus and proposed improvements ensued. Mr. Bilodeau asked why the applicant was before the CPC before the amendment was changed. Ms. Goins said the video component would be contingent on the zoning being changed. A discussion on the zoning changes ensued. Mr. Azar said the CPC had recommended approval of the zoning amendment which required that the video component of scoreboards be oriented toward the public right of way. Mr. Manjrekar read out the DPD’s staff report which found the amendment to conform to the zoning ordinance and required that the video component not be operational until the ordinance was amended. Mr. Goodman asked about the location of speakers. Ms. Em Mcmanamee said she was concerned about disturbance from the facility. Councilwoman Helen Anthony said she was concerned about noise and wanted the school to address neighborhood concerns. Mr. Amato said the speaker would be mounted on the press box and not on light poles. Mr. Dalgliesh said the school would be responsive to concerns from the community. Upon a motion by Commissioner Bilodeau seconded by Commissioner Sanchez, the CPC voted to approve the master plan amendment subject to the following condition: Operation of the video component of the scoreboard shall not be permitted until the ordinance is amended to allow for video displays on scoreboards. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: H. Bilodeau, N. Sanchez, M. Cordero, N. Verdi Abstain: M. Quezada, M. Gazdacko CITY COUNCIL REFERRAL 5. Referral no. 3

City Plan Commission Minutes of the August 19, 2025 meeting A meeting of the City Plan Commission (CPC) was held on Tuesday, August 19, 2025 at 4:45 pm in the Joseph Doorley Municipal Building, 444 Westminster Street, 1st floor Meeting Room, Providence RI 02903 A video recording of the meeting is available at: https://www.youtube.com/@pvdcpc Opening Session Call to order: Chair Michael Gazdacko called the meeting to order at 4:48 pm Members Present: Michael Gazdacko, Noel Sanchez, Charlotte Lipschitz, Miguel Quezada, Cyd McKenna Members Absent: David Caldwell, Rachael Dotson Staff Present: Robert Azar, Deputy Director, Choyon Manjrekar, Principal Planner, Sharon Garner, Deputy City Solicitor Approval of minutes from the July 15, 2025 meeting: On a motion by Commissioner Sanchez seconded by Commissioner Lipschitz, the CPC voted to approve the minutes. All voted in favor. Directors Report: Mr. Azar said the design standards committee continued to meet and would have items for review in the future. REQUEST FOR EXTENSION 1. Case no 23-065MI – 125 Tobey Street Applicant: Tobey Street LLC The applicant is requesting a two year extension to the validity of the preliminary plan – for vote (AP 35 Lot 555, Federal Hill) REQUEST FOR EXTENSION 2. Case no 23-066MI – 64 America Street Applicant: Providence Growth 2019 Fund Holdings LLC The applicant is requesting a two year extension to the validity of the preliminary plan – for vote (AP 28 Lot 819, Federal Hill) 2 REQUEST FOR EXTENSION 3. Case no 23-067MI – 20 America Street Applicant: PVD LLC The applicant is requesting a two year extension to the validity of the preliminary plan – for vote (AP 28 Lot 1046, Federal Hill) Attorney Dylan Conley presented the extension requests for all three items. He said the development on Tobey Street was intended to be an affordable development and was looking for clarity on the “eight law” with Tax Stabilization Agreements (TSA) requested for the items. He said the extensions were being requested as there was no set timeline for the City Council acting on the TSA agreements. Mr. Gazdacko asked why the final plans had not been recorded. Mr. Conley said it was due to uncertainty of the TSA agreements. Mr. Azar said the projects accompan ied zone changes to R -4 prior to the Comprehensive Plan being amended, with the projects approved under an older version of the ordinance which allows for higher density than what is currently permitted. He said the projects are vested under more permissiv e regulations. A discussion on the continuances ensued. Mr. Azar said a two year extension may be excessive. Ms. Lipschitz asked how many units would be allowed under current zoning. Mr. Azar said the R-4 zone requires 500 SF of lot area per dwelling unit. Ms. McKenna asked if there was a way to ensure the units would be affordable. Mr. Conley said there was a commitment to the units being affordable and based on the building’s design. Ms. McKenna asked about the downsides for granting the extension. Mr. Az ar said the projects would not be built under current conditions as approved. On a motion by Commissioner Lipschitz seconded by Commissioner Quezada, the CPC voted to extend the validity of the preliminary plan for 23-065MI – 125 Tobey Street by one year. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: C. Lipschitz, M. Quezada, N. Sanchez, C. McKenna, M. Gazdacko Mr. Conley said the delays for 20 and 64 America Street were due to TSA review and owner and management changes. A discussion on both developments ensued. Mr. Gazdack o said a six month extension would be sufficient for both items. Mr. Sanchez

Referral No. 3555 – Zoning Ordinance and Development Review Regulations Proponent: Department of Planning and Development 2 Review and vote on zoning changes to implement new state laws, and discussion of changes to the development review regulations to implement new state laws – for discussion and vote Mr. Azar presented the item using a memo that summarized the changes and said they would be approved by the end of the year. The changes would apply to development plan review (DPR), administrative officers, and the Downtown Design Review Committee (DDRC) which would be a body that conducts DPR. Regulations for administrative subdivisions would remain the same. Minor subdivisions would apply to creation of up to nine lots and would be reviewed administratively. The CPC would review minor subdivisions that require relief. The enabling act allows communities to set thresholds beyond what is provided in state law. Minor land development projects currently include only residential development, but the changes would allow for some mixed use with commercial to be considered minor. He said projects that required dimensional adjustments and variances would appear before the CPC. He asked if design waivers could be granted by DPD staff. Mr. Gazdacko said design waivers could be classified as major and minor. A discussion on changes ensued. Mr. Azar said there would be two categories of waivers, minor and major, where major requests would appear before the board. He said the distinction between major and minor changes would also be included in the draft of the regulations. Mr. Azar said the DDRC conducts DPR and would be considered a technical review committee. Unified Development Review is mandated for all communities and would continue without changes under the new regulations. City Plan Commission Minutes of the August 18, 2020 meeting A regular virtual meeting of the City Plan Commission (CPC) was held on Tuesday, August 18, 2020 at 4:45 pm on the Zoom platform. A video recording of the meeting is available at: https://bit.ly/31S4e3U Opening Session Call to order: Chair Christine West called the meeting to order at 4:46 pm Members Present: Christine West, Chair, Michael Gazdacko, Christian Potter, Miguel Quezada, Harrison Bilodeau and Nicole Verdi (arrived at 4:49 pm) Members Absent: Luis Torrado Staff Present: Robert Azar, Deputy Director, Kelley Salvatore, attorney to the CPC, Choyon Manjrekar, Principal Planner Approval of minutes from the June 16, 2020 meeting: Mr. Manjrekar said the minutes from the June meeting had been reviewed for use of the word ‘substantial’ to describe changes to a project, and omission of the term ‘six percent’ to quantify the reduction in the number of rooms for a hotel. He said that based on review of the transcript, it was more appropriate to describe the changes as substantive. Minutes are based on motions made at the meeting and the six percent figure was not part of the motion. Discussion of the six percent change was included in the transcript, which is part of the meeting record. Upon a motion by Commissioner Bilodeau, seconded by Commissioner Gazdacko, the CPC voted to approve the revised minutes. All voted in favor. Approval of minutes from the July 21, 2020 meeting: Mr. Gazdacko made a motion, seconded by Mr. Quezada to approve the minutes. All voted in favor. Directors report: Mr. Azar said the appeal of the hotel development at 209-217 Angell Street would be heard by the zoning board. He said the Department of Planning and Development (DPD) would kick off their study on affordable housing the following week. More details would be presented as the study progressed. REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT – MINOR LAND DEVELOPMENT PROJECT 1. Case No. 18-027MI – 473 Washington Street (Preliminary Plan) Applicant: Batwitwash LLC The applicant is seeking to reinstate the preliminary plan approval for a minor land development project to construct a four story, 21 unit residential building at 473 Washington Street. Preliminary plan approval was granted in October 2018 and has since expired – for action (AP 29 Lots 41, 42 and 481, Federal Hill) Mr. Manjrekar introduced the item and said that the CPC would vote on reinstatement followed by approval of the preliminary plan. There were some changes that had occurred to the project since it was last presented. Mr. Nicholas Hemond, an attorney, presented the item on behalf of the applicant. Mr. Eric Zuena, the project architect, presented the revised plan. He said the most significant changes were to eliminate a curtain wall and replace it with opaque material, increase the height of the parapet and to change some elements on the building façade. He continued to present the elements of the plan. Mr. Bilodeau asked if the building’s mass had changed. Mr. Zuena said there was no change except for the raised parapet wall. Mr. Manjrekar read out the DPD’s staff report which found that the revised plan met the conditions for reinstatement as 2 there were no changes to the comprehensive plan, zoning ordinance, state laws or the subject property. He said a building on site had been demolished but that was part of the original approval. Mr. Malchus Mills said he was concerned about gentrification and displacement of residents. He said he wanted to know the rents that would be charged, if rental vouchers would be accepted and what were the conditions of the project tax treaty. Mr. Hemond said he was unsure of the rents and that the project was presented to the City Council as one that would charge market rents. The conditions of the tax treaty required the applicant to pay into the parks fund. Ms. West asked Mr. Hemond about acceptance of housing vouchers and median rents in the area. Mr. Hemond said he was unsure of the policy and median rents. He said the rents would be assessed on market conditions. ACTION – Reinstatement On a motion by Commissioner Bilodeau seconded by Commissioner Verdi, the CPC voted to adopt the findings in the DPD’s staff report and to reinstate the preliminary plan approval. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: H. Bilodeau, N. Verdi, C. West, C. Potter, M. Quezada, M. Page 2 Minutes for Wednesday April 11, 2018 Cranston Zoning Board of Review WARD 4 BRIAN & MARINA FLANNERY (OWN/APP) have filed an application to construct an addition to a single family dwelling to be used as a garage and living space with restricted rear yard setbacks at 34 Oak View Drive A/P 22, Lot 76; 18,739 s.f. area, zoned A8. Applicant seeks relief per 17.92.010 Variance; Section 17.20.120 Schedule of Intensity. Application filed 3/5/18. On a motion made by Ms. Montanaro, and seconded by Mr. Buonanno, this application was Approved. Findings of Fact: 1. The existing residential use is consistent with the Comprehensive Plan Future Land Use Map that designated this area of the City as Residential, Single Family. 2. There is an existing foundation for a 20’ x 24’ garage on the back of the house. The rear yard setback of 8.7’ for the garage, conforms to the minimum Zoning 5’ rear yard setback for a garage. 3. According to the plan submitted, the proposed 14’ x 18’ living space is over a portion of the new garage, and will have a 15’ rear yard setback, where 20’ is the minimum. 4. The neighbor’s lot abutting the applicant’s rear lot line contains an in ground pool and a shed. 5. There was no testimony in opposition to the application In this case, applying the facts above to the standard for a variance, the Board further finds that the application involves a hardship that is due to the unique characteristics of the property, and is not due to a physical or economic disability of the applicant, that the hardship does not result primarily from the desire of the applicant to realize greater financial gain, will not alter the general character of the surrounding area or impair the intent or purpose of the Zoning Ordinance or the comprehensive plan, is the least relief necessary. In granting a dimensional variance, the Board finds that the hardship suffered by the owner of the subject property if the dimensional variance is not granted amounts to more than a mere inconvenience and that the Applicant met the requirements of the Zoning Code and relief from Section 17.92.010 Section 17.20.120 is granted WARD 5 CARPIONATO PROPERTIES, INC. AND ALFRED CARPIONATO (OWN), AND WEST BAY, LLC (APP) have filed an application to construct and utilize a building as an adult day care and a medical clinic at 320 Scituate Avenue, A/P 20, lots 2112 & 2116 30,322 s.f. zoned B2. Applicant seeks relief per 17.92.010 Variance; Sections 17.20.120 Schedule of Intensity, 17.20.030 Schedule of Uses. Application filed 3/12/18. Moses Ryan Ltd, Esq. Ms. Montanaro and Mr. Norcliff recused themselves; not participating in the decision. On a motion made by Ms. McFarland, and seconded by Mr. Buonanno, this application was Approved with conditions: 1. Any proposed signage must comply with the requirements allowed per the zoned lot or be approved by variance granted from the ZBR in the future. Findings of Fact: 1. The Property is located in an A-20, single family zone. 2. The commercial project received Master Plan Approval from the Plan Commission on October 3, 2017, with the condition that Zoning approval be granted for an adult day care center and medical clinic only. 3. The application is for a 5,480 square foot, single story building with 47 parking spaces. 4. The lots are surrounded on all sides (and across the street) by multi family, high density housing, and a large apartment building for the elderly. 5. The Applicant presented testimony about the project and the need for the services at this location. 6. The Applicant presented testimony of Thomas Sweeney, who was sworn in as an expert in Real Estate. 7. Mr. Sweeney testified that in his opinion should the relief not be granted, it would amount to a loss of all beneficial use to the property given the surrounding conditions and projects. 8. There was no opposition to the application. Page 3 Minutes for Wednesday April 11, 2018 Cranston Zoning Board of Review In this case, applying the facts above to the standard for a variance, the Board further finds that the application involves a hardship that is due to the unique characteristics of the property, and is not due to a physical or economic disability of the applicant, that the hardship does not result primarily from the desire of the applicant to realize greater financial gain, will not alter the general character of the surrounding area or impair the intent or purpose of the Zoning Ordinance or the comprehensive plan, is the least relief necessary. In granting a use variance, the Board finds that the hardship suffered by the owner of the subject property if the variance is not granted would be a loss of all beneficial use and therefore relief from Sections 17.20.120 Schedule of Intensity and 17.20.030 Schedule of Uses is Granted with conditions.

DD-DPR Case No. 23.30: 33 Bassett Street – Final Design Review Final design review of the proposal by Pebb Capital, to demolish the existing structures located at 33 Bassett Street, 41-45 Bassett Street, and 51 Bassett Street, and to construct a new 6-story, mixed-use building consisting of 191 residential units and one commercial unit on the site bounded by Bassett, Claverick, and Clifford Streets. Attorney Rob Stolzman and Scot Woodin, architect, appeared to discuss the project. Mr. Woodin presented the changes to the building design since the last DDRC meeting. There was some concern with the appearance of the mesh panels attached to the exterior walls of the building in some locations. Ms. Dotson commented that they looked “stuck on.” Mr. Woodin noted that they are being considered and refined, adding that they may not be there in the end. At this time public comment was taken. Paul van Zuiden, a resident of Imperial Knife Condominiums, expressed concern regarding the impact of traffic on Clifford Street. Sharon Steele, of 95 Chestnut Street, stated that she is pleased with the design, but still has concerns with Clifford Street. She added that Mr. Stolzman is working with the city to rectify the issue and is confident that will happen. With no additional comment, public comment was closed. Mr. Michie made a motion, seconded by Ms. Dotson, to grant final design approval. Members Marsella, Michie, Dotson and Garabedian voted in favor. Motion passed. Adjournment With no further business, Mr. Michie made a motion, seconded Mr. Garabedian, to adjourn the meeting at 5:36 pm. Members Marsella, Michie, Dotson and Garabedian voted in favor. Motion passed. Respectfully submitted, Christopher J. Ise Principal Planner/Administrative Oficer

Unified Development Review for Development Plan Review Application, Preliminary Plan App. No. 2025-DPR-01 Girard Avenue, TAP 3, Lot 11 Application of NRI 104-108 Girard Partnership to construct a 1,400 sq. ft. building addition containing 4 dwelling units to the westernmost building of the 3 recently constructed apartment buildings on the lot. The existing development consists of 3 multi-family residential buildings containing 6 dwelling units each. The applicant requests a Category 1 Special Use Permit to allow for the enlargement of a multi-family dwelling in the R-10 Residential district, and requests the following dimensional variances: to construct a dwelling with a 6 ft side yard setback (10 ft required), to permit a lot coverage of 22% (20% permitted), and to permit a parking area outside of the rear and side yards of the property. The applicant was represented by attorney Jay Lynch. Mr. Lynch provided an overview of the project history, and the relief being sought. Mr. Lynch stated the additional proposed units will be ADA compliant and senior units, with an elevator being provided. Various versions of this project have been in front of previous Zoning Boards and Technical Review Committees (TRC), and due to the amount of changes and the requiring of variances, Staff required the petition to go in front of TRC and Planning Board in 2025. Mr. Lynch reviewed the current plan, a building addition containing 4 units on the western- most building, bringing the proposed project up to 22 units. Mr. Lynch requested guidance on the placement of bike racks on the site. Board Member Cromwell asked if there would be crosswalks, or sidewalks lining the front of the property, which the Mr. Lynch stated that the project team has been working with the Engineering Department following TRC review, but that Engineering advised they didn’t want the sidewalk to interrupt the site’s stormwater flow. The applicant is still working on the placement of a crosswalk, and where it would connect to the site’s proposed sidewalks, and the bus stops located on Girard Ave. Acting Chair Polski opened the public comment period, but there were no members of the public in attendance to comment. Staff clarified that Planning will continue to work with Engineering to ensure if a crosswalk is approved, it will be ADA accessible. City Plan Commission Minutes of the August 19, 2025 meeting A meeting of the City Plan Commission (CPC) was held on Tuesday, August 19, 2025 at 4:45 pm in the Joseph Doorley Municipal Building, 444 Westminster Street, 1st floor Meeting Room, Providence RI 02903 A video recording of the meeting is available at: https://www.youtube.com/@pvdcpc Opening Session Call to order: Chair Michael Gazdacko called the meeting to order at 4:48 pm Members Present: Michael Gazdacko, Noel Sanchez, Charlotte Lipschitz, Miguel Quezada, Cyd McKenna Members Absent: David Caldwell, Rachael Dotson Staff Present: Robert Azar, Deputy Director, Choyon Manjrekar, Principal Planner, Sharon Garner, Deputy City Solicitor Approval of minutes from the July 15, 2025 meeting: On a motion by Commissioner Sanchez seconded by Commissioner Lipschitz, the CPC voted to approve the minutes. All voted in favor. Directors Report: Mr. Azar said the design standards committee continued to meet and would have items for review in the future. REQUEST FOR EXTENSION 1. Case no 23-065MI – 125 Tobey Street Applicant: Tobey Street LLC The applicant is requesting a two year extension to the validity of the preliminary plan – for vote (AP 35 Lot 555, Federal Hill) REQUEST FOR EXTENSION 2. Case no 23-066MI – 64 America Street Applicant: Providence Growth 2019 Fund Holdings LLC The applicant is requesting a two year extension to the validity of the preliminary plan – for vote (AP 28 Lot 819, Federal Hill) 2 REQUEST FOR EXTENSION 3. Case no 23-067MI – 20 America Street Applicant: PVD LLC The applicant is requesting a two year extension to the validity of the preliminary plan – for vote (AP 28 Lot 1046, Federal Hill) Attorney Dylan Conley presented the extension requests for all three items. He said the development on Tobey Street was intended to be an affordable development and was looking for clarity on the “eight law” with Tax Stabilization Agreements (TSA) requested for the items. He said the extensions were being requested as there was no set timeline for the City Council acting on the TSA agreements. Mr. Gazdacko asked why the final plans had not been recorded. Mr. Conley said it was due to uncertainty of the TSA agreements. Mr. Azar said the projects accompan ied zone changes to R -4 prior to the Comprehensive Plan being amended, with the projects approved under an older version of the ordinance which allows for higher density than what is currently permitted. He said the projects are vested under more permissiv e regulations. A discussion on the continuances ensued. Mr. Azar said a two year extension may be excessive. Ms. Lipschitz asked how many units would be allowed under current zoning. Mr. Azar said the R-4 zone requires 500 SF of lot area per dwelling unit. Ms. McKenna asked if there was a way to ensure the units would be affordable. Mr. Conley said there was a commitment to the units being affordable and based on the building’s design. Ms. McKenna asked about the downsides for granting the extension. Mr. Az ar said the projects would not be built under current conditions as approved. On a motion by Commissioner Lipschitz seconded by Commissioner Quezada, the CPC voted to extend the validity of the preliminary plan for 23-065MI – 125 Tobey Street by one year. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: C. Lipschitz, M. Quezada, N. Sanchez, C. McKenna, M. Gazdacko Mr. Conley said the delays for 20 and 64 America Street were due to TSA review and owner and management changes. A discussion on both developments ensued. Mr. Gazdack o said a six month extension would be sufficient for both items. Mr. Sanchez asked what would happen if the extension ran out. Mr. Gazdacko said the applicant would need to return and have the projects comply or ask for relief. On a motion by Commissioner Quezada seconded b y Commissioner Lipschitz, the CPC voted to extend the validity of the preliminary plan for 23-066MI – 64 America Street by six months. Dick Galvin, representing CV Properties, and John Sullivan, architect from Spagnolo Gisness Associates, appeared to present the project. Mr. Galvin gave an overview of the project. He went on to say that the building mass has two distinct volumes, noting the possibility of a soft glow cornice. Mr. Sullivan detailed the ground floor elevation and landscaping. Mr. Glavin stressed the importance of this building looking residential with a more successful ground floor design. Rise Above All Properties, LLC seeks approval for a Major Amendment to the approved plan for a Major Land Development project in order to construct a mixed -use multifamily structure on a 97,567 +/ - sqft (2.24 +/- acre) tract of land, zoned Conant Thread (CT), fronting on Pine Street, identified as Assessor’s Plat 53, Lots 567 and 568, and addressed a s 258 Pine Street. The proposed project is a mixed-use multifamily construction featuring 190 residential units and two commercial spaces with associated amenities. The project was previously granted final plan approval at the July 15th, 2025 Planning Comm ission meeting and now returns for a major amendment to reconfigure the site to add additional housing units and additional parking spaces while decreasing the building footprint and height. City Staff presented the application from Rise Above All Properties, LLC seeking approval for a major amendment to a previously approved plan for a Major Land Development project at 258 Pine Street. The project was previously granted Final Plan Approval at the July 15, 2025 Planning Commission meeting. The staff explained that the amendment would reconfigure the site to add additional housing units (increasing from 180 to 190 residential units), add additional parking spaces, and decrease the building footprint and height. The staff noted that the proposed project is a mixed-use multifamily construction featuring 190 residential units and two commercial spaces with associated amenities. The new site plan splits the previously approved L-shaped building into two separate buildings, which slightly shrinks the footprint while increasing parking spaces and adding landscaping throughout the site. Referral no 3594 – Amendment of section 1904 Proponent: Department of Planning and Development The proponent is proposing to amend Section 1904.E.2 of the ordinance to clarify the rules for height adjustments that may be granted for land development projects – for action Mr. Azar introduced the item which would pertain to dimensional adjustments that could be granted for land development projects. They included reducing setbacks, increasing dwelling unit density and increasing building height with applicants providing amenities that are in the public interest to qualify. The CPC had granted an extra story for a development at 128 Wayland Ave which was appealed by a neighbor. The Superior Court judge issued a decision finding that the Ordinance allowed for granting additional building height or additional stories, but not both, contrary to how the CPC has interpreted the provision. He said the City could get the judge to reconsider but amending the ordinance was the most expedient way to proceed. For example, where the ordinance reads that '12' or one story' can be granted, would be amended to read '12 not to exceed one story'. The amendment would not change the spirit of the ordinance but preserve the status quo. A discussion on the amendment ensued. On motion by Commissioner Sanchez, seconded by Commissioner Caldwell, the CPC made a positive recommendation to the City Council to approved the amendment. The CPC voted as follows: Aye: N. Presentations made by Girl Scouts of Southeastern New England CEO Dana Borrelli- Murray, architect Christina Carlson of Union Studio, and project manager Mike Russell. Mr. Monti added that the project team presented and worked with the Solicitor’s office to generate conditions of approval, which was provided to Chair Brooks. Additional paper copies were handed to Board members during the meeting. Following CEO Borelli-Murray’s presentation on site operations, Chair Brooks questioned the hosting of events on the property. Mr. Monti responded that every charitable institution in the City is permitted to rent out their facilities occasionally for accessory use, as confirmed by Zoning Officer and Soliticor. Following architect Christina Carlson’s presentation, Frederick’s Huntsberry asked what qualities this GSSNE Facility had that are not present at the other two GSSNE facilities. CEO Borelli-Murray stated this experience is smaller than other facilities, and girls are able to walk to Gooseberry Beach and have a relationship with Tall Ships organization. Chair Brooks re-opened the public hearing, continued from the June 2nd meeting. Staff presented a letter submitted by resident. Resident and prior Councilor Angela Lima spoke in support of the application. Claire McPherson, Newport resident and GSSNE board member, spoke in support. Direct abutter Rachel Connerton of 140 Carroll Ave spoke in order to reiterate concern over the property being available for outside rental. Chair Brooks closed the public hearing. The 6 application provided conditions were read. Board Member Paul McGreevy pointed out the majority of conditions were what the zoning code required anyway. Case no. 24-076UDR – 16-22 Grove Street Applicant: 16 Grove LLC The applicant is seeking preliminary plan approval for a major change to an approved subdivision with unified development review in the R-4 zone. The CPC approved a minor subdivision of the subject lot which measures approximately 7,638 SF and is occupied by two three-family dwellings, into two lots of 3,820 SF and 3,817 SF with one building on each lot. The CPC also granted associated relief for minimum lot size, minimum lot area, minimum lot width, maximum total, front and rear yard impervious surface coverage and side setback, and maximum building coverage for proposed parcel B. The applicant is requesting a major change, for relief for 56% front yard impervious coverage, 80% rear yard impervious coverage and 86% total maximum impervious coverage for lot A. Relief requested for lot B includes 57% front yard impervious coverage, and total maximum impervious coverage of 93%. The requests represent a major change from relief granted by the CPC – for vote (AP 28 Lot 901, Federal Hill) – a transcript of the item is available on request and has been made part of the record Mr. Manjrekar introduced the item. Attorney Dylan Conley presented on behalf of the applicant. A discussion on the item ensued with the CPC hearing from Mr. Conley, his expert and asking for public comment. On a motion by Commissioner Lipschitz, seconded by Commissioner Sanchez, the CPC voted to approve the requested dimensional relief. The CPC voted as follows: AYE: C. Lipschitz, N. Sanchez, D. Caldwell, M. Gazdacko Recuse: M. Quezada, R. Dotson On a motion by Commissioner Lipschitz seconded by Commissioner Sanchez, the CPC voted to approve the preliminary plan finding it to be in conformance with the zoning ordinance and comprehensive plan. The plan was approved subject to the following conditions: 1. The final plan shall clearly dimension the limits of impervious coverage on the plan with a calculation reflecting the amount of relief granted. 2. The applicant shall obtain a zoning certificate of compliance prior to final plan submission indicating installation of pervious surface in the middle of the parking spaces on Lot A and adjacent to the street tree plantings. The CPC voted as follows: AYE: C. Lipschitz, N. Sanchez, D. Caldwell, M. Gazdacko Recuse: M. Quezada, R. Dotson MAJOR LAND DEVELOPMENT PROJECT PUBLIC HEARING 3. Sanchez, D. Caldwell, C. Lipschitz, R. Dotson, M. Quezada, M. Gazdacko Upon a motion by Commissioner Caldwell seconded by Commissioner Lipschitz, the CPC voted to combine master and preliminary plan approval, having granted the requested waiver and finding that items required for both stages were submitted. Pre-Application Meeting 177 School St (AP 23 Lot 627) Charlie Adams from Penrose presented a pre-application for a mixed-income housing development at 177 School Street. He explained that Penrose is a 50-year-old owner, manager, and developer of multifamily housing active in 17 states. The New England office manages their pipeline from Connecticut through Massachusetts. Charlie Adams shared examples of their projects in the region, including Tempo in Providence and Soria in East Greenwich. The proposed project for the Tidewater site would be a 72-unit building with a podium-style design (concrete first level with five stories above). The development would serve residents between 30% and 80% of area median income, with a mix of one, two, and three-bedroom units (27 one-bedrooms, 26 two- bedrooms, and 19 three-bedrooms). The project would be located near the soccer stadium and include outdoor landscape spaces and courtyards. Liz Peabody from The Architectural Team detailed the building design, which would include parking and building services on the ground floor with residential units above. The design would break up the 200+ foot elevation with recesses and color variation to make it appear as smaller individual pockets of buildings rather than one large mass. Amenities would include shared spaces on each floor, social services, and a roof deck facing the water and stadium. Charlie Adams explained the funding would primarily come from low-income housing tax credits, state funding support, and private mortgages, with an application timeline targeting November/December 2025. Construction would follow if funding is awarded around May/June of the following year. Commission members expressed support for the project and particularly appreciated the number of family-sized units. Several commissioners suggested including even more two and three-bedroom units if possible to meet family housing needs in the community. Commissioners discussed safety considerations for children near the river, and the development team explained that the building would be elevated at the School Street level with natural barriers to the river. The site planning would incorporate pedestrian improvements and potentially a bus shelter. J. Commissioner opened the floor for public comment: Andy Mullen, 107 Johnson Street; Supports, suggested it could be even larger and include more family- sized units, noting the high demand from creditworthy families who cannot find housing. Councilman Clovis Gregor, Resident; Supports, Appreciated the developer's approach to community engagement. K. Co

Senior Planner, Grace Brownell, presented a set of proposed amendments to the Pawtucket Zoning Ordinance to regulate retail cannabis sales. The proposal would establish retail cannabis as a distinct use category, limit such establishments to the City’s two industrial zoning districts, and require special use permits through the Unified Development Review process. Additional provisions include buffer requirements from schools, parks, residential areas, and other cannabis retailers, as well as standardized hours of operation from 8:00 AM to 8:00 PM. Senior Planner Brownell presented maps showing the eligib le areas after applying these buffers, noting that the restrictions would significantly limit viable parcels for retail cannabis use. Following Senior Planner Brownell’s staff presentation, Commissioner Greenman inquired into the definition of "educationa l institution" and whether it included establishments like the Boys and Girls Club. Zoning Director Carl Johnson clarified that the definition includes K -12 schools (public, private, and Catholic) and daycares, but not facilities like the Boys and Girls Cl ub. Commissioner Greenman asked if the buffer requirements would apply to licensed childcare centers and Director Johnson stated that under state law those facilities would not be subject to the buffer requirement. Commissioner Greenman further inquired about the procedural timeline, noting that the proposal was already scheduled for the Ordinance Committee the following day. Staff confirmed this was the case and emphasized that the Planning Commission’s recommendation, while only advisory to City Council, still mattered as input that would be incorporated into the legislative decisioning of the Council. Hearing no further questions or comments, and hearing no public comments, Chairwoman Kolodziej entertained a motion for the proposed amendments to the Zoning Ordinance. Having found that the Amendment is generally consistent with the goals and purposes of the Comprehensive Plan, and serves to protect the health and general welfare of the City , and upon a motion made by Commissioner Renaud, and seconded by Commissioner Crowley, the City Planning Commission voted (5 -1) to forward a positive recommendation on the proposed amendments to the Zoning Ordinance to the Ordinance Committee. Commissioner Greenman was the sole dissenting vote.
